candidates.title: End-to-end generate→verify→repair: measuring verifier impact on LLM-generated network configurations
candidates.research_question: How much does integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate→verify→repair loop reduce safety-violating network configurations produced by an LLM compared to LLM-only proposals under matched tasks and topologies?
hypotheses: An LLM paired with a deterministic verifier plus an automated repair loop will produce significantly fewer safety violations than the same LLM producing configurations without verifier feedback.
The majority of safety improvement will be achieved within the first one or two repair iterations, yielding diminishing returns thereafter.
candidates.proposed_design: Controlled paired experiment. Use a public/synthetic corpus of intent-to-configuration tasks covering VLAN, ACL, and static-route changes across a set of canonical topologies. For each task: (1) prompt a fixed LLM to generate a device configuration change; (2) run a deterministic verifier (e.g., Batfish/Minesweeper style checks) to detect violations; (3) if violations, invoke an automated repair prompt loop constrained by verifier feedback up to N=5 iterations or until verifier passes; (4) record raw LLM-only proposal, corrected proposal, verifier traces, and repair iterations. Compare to an LLM-only arm that returns the first proposal without verifier feedback. Use fixed seeds, frozen prompts, and preregistered inclusion rules.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task records containing: initial LLM proposal, verifier pass/fail flags, number of repair iterations, final proposal, list and severity of detected violations (reachability, blackholes, ACL breaches), time per iteration, and whether final proposal passed verifier. Aggregate counts: violation rate (initial vs final), repair success rate, iterations distribution, and latency.
candidates.primary_outcome: Relative reduction in verifier-detected safety-violation rate (percentage points) from LLM-only proposals to final proposals after the verify+repair loop, measured across the task set.
candidates.analysis_outline: Paired comparison (per-task) of violation presence initial vs final using McNemar's test for binary pass/fail; compute absolute and relative risk reduction with 95% CIs. Report distribution of iterations and latency; analyze repair-success probability as function of initial violation class using logistic regression. Conduct sensitivity analyses excluding tasks where verifier cannot model the device feature. Predefine alpha=0.05 and correct for multiple property-types using Benjamini–Hochberg.
risks: Verifier–modeling mismatch causing false positives/negatives in evaluation; repair loop producing syntactically valid but semantically incompatible configs for real devices; overfitting prompts to synthetic topologies reducing external validity; resource/latency cost of repeated model calls.

candidates.title: Cross-vendor robustness of LLM intent-to-configuration translation
candidates.research_question: How reliably do LLM-based intent-to-configuration translations generalize across heterogeneous vendor CLIs (e.g., Cisco IOS, Juniper Junos, Arista EOS), and how much can lightweight prompt adaptation reduce vendor-specific error rates?
hypotheses: LLM translations will have significantly higher error rates on vendor CLIs that are underrepresented or unseen in the prompt/context compared to seen vendors.
Providing small vendor-specific prompt adapters/templates (few-shot examples or constraint templates) will significantly reduce translation errors relative to a vendor-agnostic prompt baseline.
candidates.proposed_design: Assemble a public or synthetic dataset of matched high-level intents and ground-truth vendor-specific configuration fragments for three vendors. For each intent-vendor pair run three conditions: (A) vendor-agnostic LLM prompt; (B) vendor-annotated prompt (explicit vendor token, no examples); (C) vendor-adapter prompt with 3–5 few-shot example mappings. Validate outputs syntactically and semantically via vendor-grammar checks and a verifier (where supported). Measure per-vendor accuracy, edit distance to ground truth, and actionable-error rate. Freeze prompts and seeds; preregister inclusion/exclusion rules and evaluation rubric.
candidates.expected_data: Per-case records: intent, vendor, prompt condition, generated config, syntactic parse result, semantic validation result, edit distance to ground truth, and binary actionable-success flag. Aggregates: per-vendor accuracy by condition, mean edit distance, failure-mode taxonomy (syntax vs semantic vs semantic-incorrect-but-syntactically-valid).
candidates.primary_outcome: Per-vendor actionable-success rate difference between vendor-agnostic baseline and vendor-adapter prompt condition (percentage points) with 95% CI.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compare per-vendor accuracy across conditions using mixed-effects logistic regression with random intercept for intent to account for intent difficulty. Test fixed effect of prompt condition and vendor and their interaction. Post-hoc pairwise comparisons with Tukey adjustment. Report effect sizes and bootstrapped CIs for edit-distance reductions.
risks: Public dataset limitations may not reflect proprietary vendor nuances; syntactic validators may not capture all semantic hazards; copyright/privacy constraints if real configs are used (use synthetic/public only); prompt-adapter gains may not generalize to unseen features.

candidates.title: Operational-safety metrics: predicting risk from LLM proposals using validator and rollback measures
candidates.research_question: Which operational-safety metrics derived from validator outcomes and rollback/canary simulations best predict simulated operational risk (e.g., MTTR, outage-severity) from LLM-generated NetOps changes?
hypotheses: A composite metric combining validator false-negative rate and rollback success probability will predict simulated MTTR better than task-level LLM accuracy alone.

Validator false-negative rate (violations missed by verifier) will be the single strongest predictor of severe simulated outages compared to other single metrics (edit distance, syntactic error rate).
candidates.proposed_design: Design a simulation environment that can execute proposed changes on forked topologies and simulate failure impact (reachability loss, route blackholes). For a corpus of LLM proposals, compute candidate metrics: validator true/false positive/negative rates,canary-detection probability, rollback success rate, syntactic-error rate, and LLM task-accuracy. For each proposal, run a simulated deployment protocol with canary percentage and rollback rules to record MTTR and outage severity. Use cross-validated predictive modeling to evaluate which metrics (or combinations) predict MTTR and outage severity.
candidates.expected_data: Row-level dataset: proposal id, metric vector (validator FN rate, FP rate, canary detect, rollback success prob, syntactic-error flag, LLM accuracy), simulated MTTR (minutes), simulated outage-severity score, and binary severe-outage indicator. Aggregates: correlations, model coefficients, and predictive performance (R^2/AUROC) for candidate metrics and composites.
candidates.primary_outcome: Predictive performance (adjusted R^2 for MTTR; AUROC for severe-outage) of the preregistered composite metric vs task-level LLM accuracy, demonstrating whether composite improves predictive power by a preregistered margin.
candidates.analysis_outline: Fit LASSO-regularized linear regression for MTTR and logistic regression for severe-outage with nested cross-validation. Compare nested models using likelihood-ratio tests and report bootstrapped CIs for R^2 and AUROC. Compute SHAP or feature-importance post-hoc explanations to identify dominant predictors. Prespecified threshold for improvement: composite must increase R^2 by >=0.05 over baseline to be considered practically better.
risks: Simulation fidelity may not capture real operator rollback constraints; composite metric tuned to the simulated environment may not generalize; validators may have blind spots producing misleading predictor values.

candidates.title: Bounded iterative self-correction (generate–critic) trade-offs: safety gains vs latency and oscillation
candidates.research_question: Does imposing a bounded number of critic-verified correction iterations on an LLM-based NetOps pipeline yield a practical balance between safety improvement and latency/resource cost, and where does oscillatory or divergent behavior emerge?
hypotheses: Most safety gains from iterative generate–critic repair occur within a low iteration bound (1–3 iterations), after which gains plateau while latency increases linearly.

Unbounded or poorly constrained iterative repair increases risk of oscillation (repeated semantic flips) and can produce semantic divergence; introducing a bounded stopping rule reduces oscillation frequency without materially reducing final-pass safety under standard tasks.
candidates.proposed_design: Select a representative task set of intent-to-configuration and repair problems. For each task run iterative repair experiments with iteration bounds B∈{0,1,2,3,5,10} where 0 corresponds to no repair. Use a fixed critic/verifier providing deterministic diagnostic feedback. For each B record violation rate after final iteration, total latency, number of oscillation events (measured as repeating prior configs or cycling property violations), and resource consumption (token counts/model calls). Predefine oscillation detection rules and stopping criteria. Compare bounded vs effectively unbounded (B=10) behavior.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task series: iteration index, proposal text, verifier result, diagnostic messages, timestamps, token counts, oscillation flag. Aggregates: violation rate vs B, median latency vs B, oscillation incidence vs B, and safety-per-cost ratios.
candidates.primary_outcome: Optimal bounded iteration B* that maximizes reduction in violation rate per unit latency (safety-per-latency) and the observed oscillation rate at different bounds.
candidates.analysis_outline: Plot violation rate and latency as functions of B; compute marginal safety gain per additional iteration. Use breakpoint analysis to identify B* where marginal gain falls below pre-registered threshold. Test oscillation incidence differences across B using Poisson or negative-binomial regression. Report trade-off curves and recommend bounded settings with bootstrapped uncertainty.
risks: Oscillation detection heuristics may misclassify legitimate multi-step repairs; bounded iteration recommendations may be dataset- or prompt-sensitive; latency/operational-cost findings depend on access-cost assumptions and model pricing.
